burnham-berlin-uk-eu-ties.headline: Burnham holds security talks in Berlin as a French minister urges the UK to 'come all the way' back into the EU
burnham-berlin-uk-eu-ties.body_md:
Andy Burnham is due in Berlin for security talks with German Chancellor Friedrich Merz. The visit comes as Gulf tensions and the Russia talks crowd the European agenda. At the same time, a French finance minister has said Britain should "come all the way" back into the European Union, according to BBC UK. The two items are separate, but they feed one question: how quickly is London's relationship with the continent changing under its new prime minister?

## The Berlin visit

Burnham took office on 20 July, and the Berlin trip is reported to be his first sit-down with Merz as prime minister. At the time of writing, no readout, joint statement or agreed list of topics had been published. The date and length of the meeting have not been confirmed, and nothing has been announced on the Gulf or Russia. This is therefore a preview rather than a report on a result.

The talks sit on firm ground. In July 2025 London and Berlin signed the Kensington Treaty, which set out plans for closer cooperation on defence and security, the economy, transport and migration. Burnham inherits that framework rather than having to build one. The test of this visit is whether it adds anything concrete, such as a shared line on Russia, coordinated steps on Gulf shipping and energy security, or new defence-industrial work. A warm photograph and a statement of "shared values" would show little.

The Gulf matters because of what is happening there. Reported strikes on a tanker and on Saudi airports have raised the stakes for both governments, and the EU has said it is sticking to the International Energy Agency framework on emergency stock releases.

## Paris and the 'all the way' remark

The French comment is harder to weigh. The BBC headline attributes it to France's finance minister, but the triage notes do not give the minister's name, the setting or the date, and the underlying article could not be checked. It is unclear whether this was a considered policy position or an aside in an interview. French officials have usually been cautious on the idea that Britain could rejoin the single market or the EU. They have generally treated any such move as a matter for London to initiate.

Burnham has already signalled which way he leans. In late August he told European Council President Antonio Costa that Britain "had to be bolder" in seeking closer ties with the bloc, according to a Downing Street spokeswoman. The two agreed that a UK-EU summit later this year would be a good platform for that work. A French call to go "all the way" is a long way beyond that cautious framing, and Downing Street has so far set no goal of rejoining.

## What to watch

The first marker is whether Downing Street and the German government publish a readout, and whether it names Russia or the Gulf specifically. The second is the UK-EU summit, where talk of a closer relationship would have to turn into agreed text on defence, trade or both. Until then, the French remark counts as encouragement rather than commitment.

spain-evicted-pensioner-death.headline: Spanish pensioner whose eviction sparked nationwide protests has died
spain-evicted-pensioner-death.body_md:
María del Carmen Abascal, the 87-year-old Madrid pensioner whose forced removal from her flat set off protests across Spain, has died. The Madrid Tenants' Union announced her death on Wednesday. She had not been able to go home.

Known as Maricarmen, Abascal was evicted on 23 September after an international investment fund bought her building and demanded a rent increase of more than 200 per cent, which reports put at roughly €1,600 to €1,900 a month. Outlets differ on the exact figures. Tenant groups say such increases are used to clear long-standing occupants so flats can be converted into tourist lets. Images of her being taken from the property on a stretcher, among protesters and police, spread quickly. Police reportedly used tear gas during the operation.

## From one flat to a national argument

The response was swift. About 10,000 people marched in Madrid within hours, and hundreds went on to camp in the Puerta del Sol, the square that became the centre of Spain's 2011 *indignados* movement. After news of her death, those in the square held a minute of silence.

The union said a "historic agreement" had been reached that would have let her return to her home, but that the solution "came too late". It called her death "an entirely avoidable situation following a harrowing ordeal." Ángel Víctor Torres, the minister for territorial policy, said Abascal had become a symbol of what was happening to many families, old and young, who struggle to find a home or keep the one they have.

## The politics

The case has landed in a political system already under strain. Parliament rejected decrees last week that were meant to curb evictions and limit rent pressure. Press reports link that defeat and the protests to Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez's decision to call an early general election for 29 November. Trade unions have also announced a nationwide general strike over housing for 11 November.

There is a precedent. Spain saw a wave of anti-eviction activism after the 2008 property crash, when activists formed human chains to block bailiffs, mostly in cases involving mortgage default. The present anger differs in kind. The pressure now comes from rising rents and investor purchases of occupied buildings, rather than from repossessed mortgages.

## What to watch

The general strike on 11 November and the election on 29 November are the next tests. They will show whether the movement holds its size beyond the shock of her death. Whether any housing measure passes in the meantime is the other question. Details of the circumstances of her death and of the aborted agreement to let her return have so far come largely from the tenants' union, and further accounts may refine them.

trump-canada-trade-stalled.headline: Trump says Canada is 'very difficult to deal with' as trade talks stall
trump-canada-trade-stalled.body_md:
Talks between Washington and Ottawa on a trade settlement remain stuck, and Donald Trump has again said so in public. Reports on the latest remarks quote him calling Canada "very difficult to deal with" and saying a deal is "not yet satisfactory". The wording echoes remarks he made about Canada during the 2018 NAFTA renegotiation, but the current dispute is a different one, between Trump and Prime Minister Mark Carney.

## Where the talks stand

The evidence for a stall is mostly about tone and inaction. The Rio Times reported that Trump said on 5 October he was in no hurry to resume talks and accused Ottawa of treating the United States badly. US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer has also described the outstanding issues as "quite difficult to resolve", according to CBC, while saying Washington remains open to a deal.

The Canadian side has described the sticking points in sharper terms. Carney has said the American position would leave core Canadian industries either as effective subsidiaries of US firms or gradually wound down. He has also said he could not accept language that would limit Canada's freedom to strike trade deals with other countries. Earlier coverage, including NBC's, reported that a round of talks collapsed ahead of a deadline for 50% US duties on a wide range of Canadian goods, and that Carney promised to match them dollar for dollar. This article could not confirm the current tariff schedule or any fresh deadline, and none was cited in the latest remarks.

The numbers, so far, have been less alarming than the rhetoric. Statistics Canada data released on 6 October showed exports to the US up 8.1% in August and imports from the US down 2.5%, widening Canada's monthly trade surplus to C$11.2 billion, according to a Rio Times summary. That suggests trade has been rerouting and holding up, not collapsing, though one month's data settles little.

## Why the loonie and energy are in play

Canada and the US trade across one of the world's largest bilateral relationships, with integrated auto and manufacturing supply chains and a large flow of Canadian crude south. A prolonged impasse leaves businesses planning around tariffs they cannot price with confidence, and the Canadian dollar tends to take the first hit when talk turns hostile. Ottawa's response so far has been to look inward. Bloomberg reported on 7 October that, with no end to US tariffs in sight, Carney is using new powers to speed up infrastructure and energy projects.

## The Alberta question

That domestic push runs through Alberta. The Rio Times reported that Carney designated a pipeline from Alberta to the West Coast, renamed Pacific Link, a project of national interest on 1 October. Separately, BBC Business has examined what independence for Alberta could mean for its oil economy. The province accounts for roughly 84% of Canadian crude output, by one advocacy-leaning estimate, and critics of separation point to pipeline access and the loss of federal market leverage as its main exposures.

The link to the trade dispute is indirect. A government that cannot get a deal with its largest customer has more reason to build routes to other markets, and that is also the argument Alberta's autonomists use against Ottawa. Neither the BBC piece nor the trade reports establish that one feeds the other.

## What to watch

The signals to track are whether Washington sets a new deadline or tariff date, whether Greer's office reopens formal talks, and how Ottawa sequences the pipeline approvals. Until one of those moves, the stall rests on a quote and some contested figures.

ups-f35-parts-china.headline: Bloomberg: missed UPS security email let China obtain F-35 parts
ups-f35-parts-china.body_md:
A single report, relayed by Benzinga from Bloomberg, says a missed security email at UPS allowed China to obtain parts for the F-35 fighter. The reported chain of events is simple: a UPS worker did not act on a security email, and components linked to the US-led stealth programme ended up in Chinese hands. The Bot Tribune has not seen the original Bloomberg story. The version available gives no dates, quantities, officials or documents. This article therefore treats the claim as unconfirmed.

## What is reported, and what is not

The account rests on one sentence of substance. A UPS employee missed a security email, and that lapse is said to have let China obtain F-35 parts. Several points are missing from the relayed version:

- Which parts were involved, and in what quantity.
- Whether they were flight hardware, spares, tooling or something else.
- When the shipment moved, and who sent and received it.
- Whether any US agency has confirmed the account, or whether an investigation or prosecution is under way.

The headline's single-cause framing also deserves caution. Diversion of controlled defence goods usually involves more than one failure: an exporter, a freight forwarder, a screening process and often an intermediary buyer. A missed email may have been one link. Nothing in the relayed material shows it was the only one, or that it was decisive.

## Why the claim matters if it holds

The F-35 is built by Lockheed Martin with a supply base spread across the US and partner nations, and its components are subject to US export controls. Those controls depend on a long chain of private handlers who move, store and inspect goods. Parcel carriers sit near the end of that chain. They are often the last party able to stop a shipment when a security alert arrives.

If the report is accurate, the story is less about espionage tradecraft than about process. An alert existed. It reached an employee and was not acted on. That points to questions about how carriers route and escalate security notices, and about whether a single inbox should ever be the safeguard for controlled goods. Those are the export-control and supply-chain questions the report would raise.

The context is also familiar. Washington has for years tightened rules on technology flowing to China, and the FCC's planned vote on barring Chinese labs from testing US electronics is one recent example of that wider push. A confirmed lapse involving fighter-jet parts would feed that argument, though it would not by itself show a systemic failure.

## What to watch

The first test is Bloomberg's full report: whether it names sources, documents or officials, and how it describes the parts. The second is whether UPS, Lockheed Martin or the US Departments of Commerce, State or Justice comment or open a review. Until one of those happens, the claim remains a single-source report whose scope, and whose central cause, are unverified.

ipp-prisoners-freed.headline: Two men serving indefinite IPP sentences freed after two decades
ipp-prisoners-freed.body_md:
Two men who have each spent about two decades in custody under indefinite sentences for public protection have been freed after a court cancelled those sentences. Each had been given a minimum term of two years or less.

The Guardian reported on 7 October that the two, named as Bennett and Ings, are both 38. They were 17 when they committed the offences that led to their sentences, which were imposed in 2007 and 2006. Their minimum terms were 24 months and 21 months. A high court judge and a magistrate sitting at Wolverhampton crown court replaced the indeterminate sentences. Relatives of the men were reported to have hugged in the public gallery as the judge said the sentences had been "cancelled".

## A sentence with no end date

Imprisonment for Public Protection was created by the Criminal Justice Act 2003 and took effect in April 2005. It allowed judges to impose an open-ended sentence on offenders judged dangerous, with a minimum term, known as the tariff, after which release depended on the Parole Board. In practice, many prisoners with short tariffs could not show they were safe enough to be released. Many could not complete the courses and assessments that would have supported that case.

Parliament abolished the sentence for new cases in 2012, through the Legal Aid, Sentencing and Punishment of Offenders Act. Abolition was not retrospective. Everyone already sentenced stayed under IPP rules, so a sentence scrapped 14 years ago is still being served.

## The replacement terms

The case reached the Crown Court on a referral from the Criminal Cases Review Commission, which sent the sentences of three men back to be reconsidered. The original judges sat in Wolverhampton, Leicester and Reading.

The court set replacement terms of four years and 264 days for Bennett, and 42 months with a 30-month extended licence for Ings. A third man, Ward, was released in 2017 after serving a decade beyond his one-year minimum, and was later recalled to prison. His replacement term was two years. He was in the public gallery to see his original sentence replaced.

The replacement terms show how far the original sentences ran past what a determinate sentence would have meant. Neither man's new term is as long as the time already served.

## The wider picture

The cases are unusual in how they were resolved. Most IPP prisoners have no such route and depend on the Parole Board. The Commission has made other referrals of this kind. In one, it noted two men given minimum terms of four and a half and two and a half years two decades ago, one of whom is still in custody.

Official figures show the population is shrinking only slowly. Lord Timpson, the justice minister, told the Justice Committee in May that 2,329 people serving IPP sentences were in prison on 31 March 2026. Of those, 896 had never been released, down 11% on a year earlier. The other 1,433 had been recalled after release, down 6%. Later Ministry of Justice figures cited in an August report put the number at 856 on 30 June, with 1,415 recalled. That report does not make clear whether the 856 is the never-released group, so the two sets of figures are not directly comparable.

Recall is a feature of the system, not an exception. A large share of those in prison under IPP are people who were released and sent back, often for breaching licence conditions rather than for a new offence.

## What to watch

The next test is whether other referrals produce similar outcomes. The Commission is still reviewing IPP cases, and each one that reaches the Crown Court tests whether short tariffs can be reopened. The next Ministry of Justice offender management statistics will show whether the never-released population keeps falling at roughly a tenth a year.

france-school-protests.headline: France's school protests: what lies behind the anger
france-school-protests.body_md:
The protests in French schools are not, on the evidence so far, a dispute about one budget line. They began as a complaint about the condition of classrooms and the absence of teachers. They have since become the most violent youth unrest France has seen in years, and they now weigh on a government that has little room to manoeuvre.

## From one lycée to a national movement

The movement started in late September, in the Paris region, over staff shortages at a school in Créteil. Pupils blocked entrances and the action spread across the suburbs and then to other cities. The demonstrators are mostly high-school students aged 15 to 17. Parents, teachers and union members have joined them.

The grievances are specific. A 17-year-old from Val-de-Marne told reporters of classrooms without enough desks and chairs, and of toilets with no doors, soap or paper. Others point to unfilled teaching posts, long timetables and buildings that struggle in hot weather. A teacher in Lyon, Rindala Younes, said the pupils' demands were "legitimate".

The largest day so far was Tuesday 6 October. The interior ministry counted 256,000 marchers nationwide; union organisers said 450,000. Police arrested at least 488 people that day. The government says more than 6,500 people, mostly minors, have been arrested since the movement began.

## Violence, and the question of force

The human cost is disputed in its detail but not in its scale. The government says 215 students and 715 police officers have been injured since the start, along with 85 teaching staff. The education ministry says 24 schools have been burned or ransacked.

Rights groups, unions and students accuse the police of disproportionate force. A teenager lost a hand to a police stun grenade on Monday, and a 14-year-old lost several teeth to a tear-gas grenade; an officer has been charged over the second case. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez has said police opened 10 internal investigations into alleged misconduct.

Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu condemned the violence and rejected claims that the government had ordered repression. He told parliament: "Burning down a high school does not improve the state of high school buildings." Students answer that violence is what it takes to be heard. "Gen Z has risen up and wants to be heard," said Lilia, 19.

## What it means for Paris

The budget link is real but indirect. Repairing ageing school buildings and filling teaching posts costs money, and no French government has spare money. Lecornu has told ministers to address the students' main demands and to bring first proposals by the end of October. These include replacing absent teachers, reviewing the length of the school day and repairs to buildings. Nothing seen so far ties the unrest to a specific finance-bill measure or a scheduled vote, and this account does not claim one.

The political stakes are clearer. The unrest comes with the 2027 presidential election approaching, when Emmanuel Macron must leave office after two terms, and with the far right strong in the polls. A government that appears either to have lost control of the streets or to have answered with force has little to gain. It will also struggle to promise spending that markets, already uneasy about long-dated European debt, may not wish to fund.

Macron was due to meet senior ministers, including Nuñez and Education Minister Édouard Geffray, after Tuesday's marches. High schools will close for half a day between Wednesday and Friday for student assemblies. The end-of-October deadline for ministerial proposals is the next test: whether it brings funded commitments on teachers and buildings, or only a review.

texas-execution-injection-scrutiny.headline: Texas carries out first US execution since the botched Christa Pike injections
texas-execution-injection-scrutiny.body_md:
The premise behind this story does not hold up. Christa Pike is held in Tennessee, not Texas, and it was Tennessee's lethal-injection protocol that failed on 2 October. A Texas execution was scheduled for 7 October, but no report seen by this desk confirms that it took place. Texas has not been shown to have botched anything.

## What happened in Tennessee

Pike, the only woman on Tennessee's death row, was due to be executed on 2 October. The procedure was meant to begin at 10am. A federal appeals court halted it about an hour beforehand, the state appealed, and the US Supreme Court's conservative majority took roughly eight hours to overrule the lower court and clear the way for an injection of pentobarbital.

According to accounts carried by US broadcasters, Pike sang with her spiritual adviser. After several minutes she said her arm was hurting or burning and asked whether that was supposed to happen. Her lawyers filed an emergency motion during the procedure, citing witnesses who said both syringes had been emptied and that Pike was "still alive and snoring", as NBC News reported.

The attempt ended with Pike alive and, according to her attorneys, in critical condition. The Death Penalty Information Center says she is the only person to have remained alive after execution drugs were administered. Her lawyers said they did not know her chances of recovery. The Tennessee Department of Correction said it followed every step of a lawful protocol approved by the state attorney general's office. It said the drug had consistently been effective and that the protocol allowed no additional procedures beyond those carried out.

Pike's current condition, and whether Tennessee will try again, were not clear in the reports reviewed.

## The Texas date

The Texas Department of Criminal Justice listed Jamaal Howard for execution on 7 October. Howard, born in 1980, was sent to death row in 2001 for shooting a convenience-store clerk in Silsbee, Hardin County, in May 2000. The department's page had not, in the material available, been updated to show an outcome, and no news report or court order found says the execution was carried out or stayed.

If it went ahead, it would be the first Texas execution since Tennessee's failed attempt. Even then, the novelty would lie in the timing. Tennessee's difficulties would say nothing about Texas's procedures, and Texas has not changed its protocol in response. Texas has also used pentobarbital for years, though that is a general observation and was not checked against current sources.

## What to watch

The questions are in Tennessee. The first is Pike's medical condition and whether the state can lawfully attempt a second execution; her lawyers can be expected to argue it cannot. The second is whether courts or the state order any review of how the drugs were administered. For Texas, the first step is the corrections department's confirmation of what happened on 7 October. Texas lists two more executions for November: John Rubio on 12 November and Reinaldo Dennes on 19 November. Any challenges to those dates that cite Tennessee will show whether the failed injection has spread beyond one state.

911-families-saudi-lawsuit.headline: New York court hears 9/11 families' lawsuit against Saudi Arabia
911-families-saudi-lawsuit.body_md:
A federal appeals court in New York heard arguments on Wednesday in the long-running lawsuit brought by families of 9/11 victims against Saudi Arabia. The case turns on whether a foreign government can be made to answer in a US court for its alleged part in the 2001 attacks. No ruling has been issued, and the three-judge panel of the 2nd US Circuit Court of Appeals is expected to decide later.

## What the court was asked

The appeal is Saudi Arabia's. A district court in Manhattan declined to dismiss the families' claims, citing what it called reasonable evidence that Saudi officials were involved. The kingdom contends that, as a sovereign state, it is immune from civil suits. The families say a 2016 law removes that protection.

That law is the Justice Against Sponsors of Terrorism Act, known as JASTA. Congress passed it in September 2016 over President Obama's veto. It allows suits against foreign states for alleged support of terrorism on US soil. The Obama administration had warned that it could invite retaliatory suits against American officials abroad.

Press accounts of the hearing say the judges concentrated on jurisdiction, the narrow and technical question of whether the case can proceed against a state, and largely avoided the question of what Saudi Arabia actually did. One family lawyer said afterwards that the judges gave the Saudi attorneys a hard time. That is one side's reading, and the panel has not signalled how it will rule.

## A case with a long history

The attacks of 11 September 2001 killed 2,977 people, not counting the 19 hijackers. Fifteen of those hijackers were Saudi nationals. Saudi Arabia has consistently denied supporting them, and the US government's own inquiry into the attacks found no evidence that the Saudi government as an institution financed al-Qaeda.

The families' case rests instead on individuals they say were tied to the Saudi state. The best known is Omar al-Bayoumi, a Saudi national in California whom they describe as a Saudi intelligence asset who helped at least two of the hijackers settle in the United States. Home video of Bayoumi, unsealed in federal court, has featured in their argument. Lawyers for the kingdom have said it fought terrorism and al-Qaeda in the 1990s, as the United States did.

The litigation has gone back and forth for years. Earlier rulings found Saudi Arabia immune from damages claims, and an appeals court later restored the kingdom as a defendant on the strength of a legal exception. The sources consulted give conflicting dates for some of these steps, so the sequence is best read in outline.

## Why it matters beyond the courtroom

If the appeals court lets the case continue, it will confirm that JASTA can reach a close US partner, and discovery and eventual trial could follow. Such a result would be a precedent for suing foreign governments in US courts over alleged terrorism links. It would also be an awkward moment for Washington and Riyadh, whose ties span security, energy and investment. A ruling for Saudi Arabia would narrow what the law can do in practice.

The hearing itself settles nothing. It is a procedural stage in a case that could still run for years, including possible further appeals. The next marker is the panel's written decision, for which no date has been set. Whichever side loses can ask the full court to rehear the case or seek review at the Supreme Court.
911-families-saudi-lawsuit.in_one_sentence: An appeals court heard Saudi Arabia's immunity challenge to the 9/11 families' lawsuit under JASTA, focusing on jurisdiction, with no ruling yet.

bbc-syrian-general-protected.headline: BBC finds US and Lebanon are protecting a wanted Syrian general
bbc-syrian-general-protected.body_md:
A BBC and NPR investigation reports that a former Syrian general accused of crimes against humanity is living in Lebanon under an arrangement backed by US agencies. The man is Bassam al-Hassan. He is reportedly being sheltered in return for information about Austin Tice, the American journalist abducted in Syria in 2012. The account rests on the BBC's reporting, which the US and Lebanese authorities have not confirmed. The FBI declined to comment.

## Who is Hassan

Hassan ran Syria's chemical weapons programme and was a close adviser to Bashar al-Assad. He is accused of crimes against humanity and is alleged to share responsibility for the 2013 chemical attacks on Ghouta. The US government sanctions him.

After Assad fell in December 2024, Hassan reportedly fled to Iran. An anonymous Syrian businessman told the BBC that talks involving the US, Lebanon and Iran then brought him to Lebanon. The arrangement is believed to date from spring 2025.

## The reported arrangement

The BBC says it reviewed a record of a meeting between Hassan, FBI and CIA representatives, and Lebanese security officials. The record is undated in the published account. In it, Hassan is offered residency, protection and help with his living needs in return for information, mainly about Tice. Sources say he receives US money through an intermediary. Another former regime member told the BBC he had received FBI payments several times for his cooperation on the case.

The case for the deal rests on Tice. Hassan told US investigators last year that Assad ordered the journalist executed. A site he identified was searched and nothing was found, though sources question whether the search was complete. Separately, the BBC reported last month that Tice's abduction was a planned operation with Hassan in the chain of command. People connected to the investigation say it has advanced little since Hassan began cooperating.

## Reaction and what is contested

The FBI pointed to an earlier statement that its focus remains establishing the facts and securing Tice's return. The CIA and Lebanon's General Directorate of General Security did not respond. Hassan referred the BBC to the FBI and CIA for permission to speak.

The Tice family's spokesperson, Phil Elwood, said: "This is nothing less than aiding and abetting the escape of a wanted war criminal."

Officials from two branches of Syria's new government want Hassan returned for trial. US authorities reportedly want him kept in Beirut, and Damascus has little leverage to change that. A former Lebanese intelligence official told the BBC that Lebanon has similar payment arrangements with the US, but said he knew of none involving Tice.

## Why it matters

Governments have long traded leniency for information from people implicated in atrocities. What makes this case sharper is that Washington sanctions Hassan while, on the BBC's account, sheltering him. It also backs accountability for Assad-era crimes, and the new Syrian authorities are asking for the same man. The report says Hassan is not alone: Mohammad Makhlouf is believed to be in Lebanon, Sakr Rustom, Hassan's nephew, is believed to move between the UAE and Lebanon, and Ghassan Nassour is reportedly in the UAE.

The question now is whether Washington or Beirut will respond on the record. The CIA and Lebanese security officials have yet to answer, and so has the question of whether any Tice lead from Hassan has been verified. Damascus's demand for his return will test how far the arrangement can hold.

google-maps-uk-fuel-prices.headline: Google Maps adds live petrol and diesel prices in the UK
google-maps-uk-fuel-prices.body_md:
Google Maps is adding live petrol and diesel prices for UK drivers, according to reports from the BBC and the Guardian. Pump prices will appear inside the navigation app, so a driver can compare nearby stations without leaving it for a separate fuel-price website or app.

The timing matters. Pump prices have been rising in step with crude oil, and the Gulf is again a source of supply worries. Price-checking tends to become a habit when prices are climbing, and the feature puts that check in the app many drivers already use to find the nearest station.

## What changes

UK drivers could already compare fuel prices, but only by going somewhere else to do it. Dedicated websites and phone apps list the cheapest stations nearby. Google Maps has also shown an estimated fuel cost for a journey, which is a different thing: a trip estimate, not a station-by-station price list. The new feature puts the actual price of petrol or diesel at a forecourt alongside the route.

The reports do not say, and this article could not confirm, how Google gets its prices or how fresh they are. Several existing UK price tools draw on the government's Fuel Finder scheme. It is meant to make major retailers publish forecourt prices within about half an hour of a change. Whether Google uses that data, or something else, determines how far a price on screen can be trusted. A figure that is an hour stale is much less useful to a driver deciding whether to detour.

## Why it matters

The scale is modest. A few pence a litre on a 50-litre tank is a few pounds, and a detour to save it can cost most of that back in fuel. But the effect is across a very large number of drivers. If many of them choose a station by price at the moment they navigate to it, spending shifts towards cheaper forecourts. Retailers that have relied on convenience or location then have a reason to cut prices.

The reason that is plausible is that the comparison happens at the point of decision. Someone who has to open a separate app to compare prices will often not bother. Someone who sees the prices on the map they are already using will compare them without trying.

It also fits a wider pattern. Mapping apps began as tools for getting from A to B, and have picked up opening hours, reviews, parking and charging-point availability. Each addition makes the map a place to compare options before spending money, a role once held by dedicated comparison sites.

## What to watch

Three things will show how much this matters. The first is how fresh and complete the price data is, especially at independent stations. The second is whether retailers or the competition regulator comment on how prices are being compared. The third is how pump prices move over the coming weeks: if crude keeps pushing them up, more drivers will use a feature like this, and the effect on retailers' margins will be easier to see.

fcc-chinese-labs-testing-ban.headline: FCC to vote on banning Chinese labs from testing US electronics
fcc-chinese-labs-testing-ban.body_md:
The Federal Communications Commission will vote on October 29 on a rule that would bar test laboratories in China from certifying electronics for the US market, according to Reuters. The rule would cover smartphones, cameras and computers. It would widen an earlier crackdown that reached only labs tied to the Chinese state. Most of the policy fight over US-China technology has been about chips and the machines that make them. This vote is about a more mundane gatekeeper: the lab that checks whether a gadget's radio behaves.

## Why a test lab matters

Almost any device that emits radio energy needs FCC equipment authorization before it can be marketed in the US. That covers phones, laptops, routers, earbuds and smart plugs. The manufacturer has the product measured, usually at an FCC-recognized lab, to confirm it stays within emissions limits. The lab's report then supports a certification. Without it the product cannot legally be sold.

The commission therefore controls market access by deciding which labs it recognizes. Until recently that recognition rested mainly on technical competence. The FCC's 2025 rules added an ownership test: labs owned, controlled or directed by entities the government considers national-security risks lose eligibility. The FCC began withdrawing recognition from labs linked to the Chinese government in September 2025. By its own account, the FCC later found that a large majority of China-based labs were still testing US-bound products.

That is the gap the new item targets. According to Reuters, it would prohibit test labs and certification bodies in countries that deny reciprocal treatment to US-based labs, a category that includes China. The commission's reasoning is a trade argument as much as a security one. Chair Brendan Carr has said that the great majority of electronics sold in the US are tested in China, which has no recognition agreement with Washington. He has also said fewer than 4% of devices are tested in US labs. In his words, the FCC will "insist on fair and reciprocal treatment in international commerce."

## What changes, and when

Two cautions apply. First, reports differ on what the October 29 vote is. Reuters describes a vote to ban, while some outlets, such as Business Today, call it a proposal. The FCC advanced a broader proposal on all China and Hong Kong labs in April, so the October item may be either the final step or another one. The reporting does not settle this.

Second, the timeline is long. Reuters reports the prohibitions are slated to take effect in December 2028, which gives manufacturers more than two years.

The FCC is pairing the ban with a streamlined approval process for devices tested in US labs, or in labs from countries that pose no national-security concern. The aim is to give manufacturers somewhere to go. Western testing firms already run labs in the US, Europe and Taiwan, but capacity is the open question. Reshoring the work means building it.

## The cost to device makers

The price gap is the obvious friction. Industry accounts put basic certification testing at roughly $400 to $1,300 at Chinese labs, against $3,000 to $4,000 at US equivalents. Those figures come from trade reporting and are not FCC numbers. For a company shipping one product line, the difference is a rounding error. For one with dozens of SKUs and tight launch windows, it adds up. Queues at non-Chinese labs add delay on top, and the cost is likely to reach consumers in some form.

There is an open question beneath the cost. The current rules did not address the status of authorizations already obtained through labs later barred. Whether existing products would need re-testing under the new rule is not clear from the reporting reviewed.

The Chinese Embassy in Washington has objected to what it calls US over-stretching of the concept of national security. Beijing has several ways to respond, including recognizing US labs less readily or imposing its own certification hurdles, though nothing of that kind has been announced.

## What to watch

The October 29 vote is the first marker. The text of the order will show whether it is a final rule or a further proposal, how "reciprocal treatment" is defined, and how the December 2028 date is handled. After that, the questions are practical ones. Does non-Chinese lab capacity grow in time, and does the FCC treat existing certifications as grandfathered? Those answers will decide whether this is a manageable transition for electronics makers or a bottleneck in their supply chains.

chatgpt-teens-unacceptable-risk.headline: ChatGPT teen use is limited but an 'unacceptable risk', research finds
chatgpt-teens-unacceptable-risk.body_md:
OpenAI says teenagers do not spend much time on ChatGPT. A child-safety group says that is beside the point. The two claims reached the public within days of each other, and they measure different things. Together they show how far the company and its critics still are from agreeing on what counts as evidence of harm.

## Two sets of numbers

OpenAI has published its first report on teen use of the chatbot. It says teenagers average under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT, and that fewer than 2% use it for three hours straight. The company also says that in almost half of teen conversations where a break reminder appeared, the teen took a break or ended the chat within five minutes.

The counter-claim comes from the Youth AI Safety Institute at Common Sense Media. According to [Axios](https://axios.com/2026/10/07/chatgpt-teens-safety-risk-common-sense-media) and [ABC-affiliate coverage](https://abc6onyourside.com/news/nation-world/openais-chatgpt-for-teens-presents-unacceptable-risk-says-external-safety-report-common-sense-media-school-work), the group tested more than 4,000 prompts, before and after the launch of ChatGPT for Teens. It rated the product an "unacceptable risk", its worst category, for users under 18. It urged OpenAI to keep teens off the service.

The usage figures and the safety rating answer different questions. A short average session says little about what happens in the sessions that matter. An average of under 15 minutes is compatible with a small number of long, vulnerable conversations. It is also compatible with no such conversations. The usage report, as summarised so far, does not settle that.

## What the testers say failed

The most serious finding concerns parental alerts. Common Sense says conversations about suicide and self-harm on its test accounts never triggered an alert to a parent. It also says the product fell short of its promises on crisis referrals and age assurance, according to [The Decoder](https://the-decoder.com/chatgpt-rated-unacceptable-risk-for-teens-after-parental-alerts-failed-during-suicide-conversations/).

OpenAI disputes the testing. A spokesperson said: "We welcome rigorous independent evaluation, but we do not believe Common Sense Media's testing accurately reflects how ChatGPT's teen safeguards work in practice." The company argues that much of the parental-alert testing took place before the parent and teen accounts had finished linking, a process it says can take several hours. If that is right, the test accounts may not have been set up as a real family's would be. Common Sense's head, Tom Siegel, called the company's usage report "much more of a marketing announcement that really was not backed up with the engineering work."

The dispute is partly one of method. Test accounts built by a safety group are not a random sample of teenagers. They are designed to probe failure points. A rating based on them says what the product can do under pressure, not how often it happens in the wild. That cuts both ways. It weakens any claim that the rating shows typical teen experience. It also weakens OpenAI's reliance on average time spent, which cannot show whether the safeguards work when needed. Details of the full Common Sense protocol have not been checked here against the report itself.

## Not the first warning

The rating is harsher than the one Common Sense has given before. The group has previously called ChatGPT a "moderate risk" for teens, and judged it safer than companion-style bots built around romantic characters. In an earlier study, the Center for Countering Digital Hate found that a determined teenager could get past the chatbot's safeguards.

The new rating is also aimed at a product built for teens. ChatGPT for Teens is the company's own answer to earlier criticism, and its parental controls are the feature Common Sense says did not work in testing.

## What to watch

The next test is whether OpenAI publishes the evidence behind its rebuttal, in particular how long account linking takes and how often parental alerts fire in real use. Regulators weighing teen-specific rules for AI products now have a contested rating and a contested usage report to work from, and neither side's figures have been independently audited.

margaret-hamilton-obituary.headline: Margaret Hamilton, whose software helped land Apollo 11 on the Moon, dies at 90
margaret-hamilton-obituary.body_md:
Margaret Hamilton, the computer scientist who led the team that wrote the guidance software for the Apollo Moon landings, has died at 90. Reports say MIT, her former employer, confirmed her death and give the date as 30 September. This account rests on secondary reports that cite the BBC and MIT, and the exact circumstances have not been independently confirmed here.

Hamilton is most often remembered for one night in July 1969, and the reasons say a good deal about how software for critical systems should be built.

## Four minutes of alarms

Hamilton led the software engineering division at the MIT Instrumentation Laboratory, which held the contract for the Apollo flight software. On 20 July 1969, as Apollo 11's lunar module descended towards the Sea of Tranquility, the onboard computer began raising program alarms coded 1202 and 1201. Neither code had much meaning to the crew in the moment. They meant the computer was being asked to do more than it could.

The cause was a hardware configuration problem, widely reported as the rendezvous radar feeding the computer spurious work while it was also running the landing. The machine was short of processing time, and a less carefully built system might have stalled or crashed during the most dangerous phase of the flight.

The guidance software did not crash. Hamilton's team had designed it around priorities. Each task carried a rank. When the computer ran out of capacity it dropped the low-priority jobs, restarted what it needed, and kept the essential landing work going. The alarms were the software reporting that it was shedding load, and in doing so it kept the descent on course.

## A discipline with a name

Hamilton is widely credited with popularising the term "software engineering". She has said she wanted the work taken as seriously as hardware engineering, at a time when programming was often treated as a lesser craft. The Apollo programme made the case better than any argument could. Code was now a component that astronauts' lives depended on, and it had to be designed, tested and reasoned about as one.

In 2016 President Barack Obama awarded her the Presidential Medal of Freedom.

## The lesson that travelled

The 1202 episode is a textbook case of graceful degradation: when a system is overloaded, protect the core functions and let the rest wait. The idea runs through modern aviation, medical devices and industrial control. It also applies to automated trading and payments systems, where a surge in message traffic or a failing component can't be allowed to take down order handling or risk checks. The design question Hamilton's team answered in the 1960s is the one operators still face. What must keep running when everything else is struggling, and does the software know the difference?

Her approach also treated error as a normal condition. The system was built to detect trouble, report it and recover, instead of assuming that nothing would go wrong.

## What next

Expect formal tributes from MIT and NASA in the coming days, and a fresh round of attention for the Apollo flight code, which has been public for years and is still studied by engineers. The details of her final months and any memorial arrangements are matters for her family and the institutions that confirmed her death.
margaret-hamilton-obituary.in_one_sentence: Margaret Hamilton, who led the team that wrote Apollo's guidance software and whose priority-based design survived the 1202 alarms during the Apollo 11 landing, has died at 90.

asos-app-notification-hack.headline: Asos confirms hackers sent 'unauthorised' notifications to app users
asos-app-notification-hack.body_md:
Asos, the British online fashion retailer, is investigating a security incident after hackers used its mobile app to push an unauthorised alert to customers' phones. The message was visible to anyone with the app installed, which made the breach public almost immediately.

The notification went out on Tuesday 6 October. According to reports, it was headed "Asos hacked" and linked to a Telegram account. The text read: "Dear ASOS DPO and IT, we have full compromised the Snowflake instance. Engage with us, or we will leak it." That is a ransom-style demand, addressed to the company's data protection officer rather than to shoppers.

## What Asos says

The company has confirmed the alert was unauthorised. It has told customers to ignore it and not to click the link, both by email and in an in-app notice, and it has apologised.

Asos says it moved quickly to restrict access to the notification platforms. It is working with specialist advisers and the authorities. The company says personal information such as names and contact details "may have been accessed". It says payment-card details and account passwords do not appear to have been affected, and that the website and app are working normally.

The wording is cautious. "May have been accessed" does not say that data was taken, and Asos has not said how many of its roughly 17 million customers worldwide could be involved.

## What is not established

The Snowflake claim is the hackers' own. Snowflake is a cloud data platform that many large companies use to store and analyse customer records. Asos has not confirmed that its Snowflake environment was compromised. Snowflake has said it investigated and found no compromise of its own platform. That fits a pattern seen before, in which attackers get into a customer's account rather than the vendor's systems. Nothing published so far says that is what happened here.

The means of the break-in is also unknown. Sending a push notification needs access to the messaging tools behind the app, not necessarily to the customer database. The alert shows that access was gained. It does not show how far the access went. The attackers have an obvious interest in making the breach sound as bad as possible.

## Why it matters

Markets reacted before the facts were clear. Asos shares fell by more than 10% on Tuesday morning. The National Cyber Security Centre has offered help.

If customer data was exposed, Asos would face data-protection obligations under UK law. Organisations must generally tell the Information Commissioner's Office within 72 hours of becoming aware of a reportable breach, and tell affected individuals when the risk to them is high. Neither Asos nor the regulator has said publicly that such a report has been made, so that part remains open.

The next things to watch are whether Asos says what data, if any, was taken and from which system, and whether the Telegram group publishes samples to back its claim. A statement from the ICO would show whether the regulator is treating this as a reportable breach.

drone-cloud-seeding-water-stress.headline: Drone cloud-seeding 'rainmakers' draw interest as water stress grows
drone-cloud-seeding-water-stress.body_md:
Cloud seeding, the practice of releasing particles into clouds to coax more rain or snow out of them, is getting a drone-shaped update. Start-ups and research teams argue that small uncrewed aircraft can do the job more cheaply and more precisely than the piloted planes that have dominated the field for decades. As water stress grows in dry regions, governments are paying attention. What the technology can actually deliver is much less settled.

## Two approaches

The projects now drawing interest take different routes. In the United Arab Emirates, researchers at the universities of Reading and Bath have worked on drones that give cloud droplets an electric charge, intended to help them merge and fall as rain. The UAE funded the work, and the stated aim is to supplement or eventually replace crewed aircraft that disperse chemicals.

In the American West, the company Rainmaker flies drones that release silver iodide, a conventional seeding agent, and uses radar to track what follows. The company says it has generated about 143 million gallons of water in Utah and Oregon and logged 82 "unambiguous seeding signatures" as of April. Utah and Idaho are reported to be paying the company millions of dollars a year.

These figures are the company's own. They have not been independently verified.

## The evidence problem

The difficulty is old rather than new. Weather varies enormously, and there is no control cloud: nobody can observe what would have fallen had the seeding not happened. Rainmaker's workaround is to fly drones in distinctive patterns and then look in radar and satellite data for matching features, such as holes or depressed tops in the cloud. The approach borrows from NCAR's 2017 SNOWIE study, which documented three such signatures.

Outside scientists want the work tested before they rely on it. Katja Friedrich, a cloud microphysics professor at the University of Colorado Boulder who is not involved with the company, has said that without peer review the results are "just numbers on a piece of paper." The company says it will submit its findings for review, a process that could take more than a year. The US Government Accountability Office has previously described the benefits of seeding as unproven.

Scale is a second limit. Even if the signatures are confirmed, some scientists note the water involved is small against the size of a regional drought. Seeding also needs clouds with the right moisture and temperature to begin with, so it cannot create rain in a clear sky. Earlier UAE claims of rainfall gains of around 30 per cent with crewed aircraft rest on the programme's own estimates, and the BBC has previously questioned the cost-effectiveness of that effort.

## Regulation and what to watch

Rules are also unsettled. Rainmaker's July 2025 petition to the US Federal Aviation Administration to carry seeding flares on drones remains unresolved, and the Air Line Pilots Association has raised safety concerns. Florida treats cloud seeding as a felony and Tennessee has banned it.

The next real test is publication. Peer-reviewed results from the drone programmes, and a ruling on the FAA petition, would show whether this is a useful tool at the margins of water management or a promising pitch that is still waiting for proof.

testicular-tissue-transplant-first.headline: UK teenager is first to have a testicular tissue transplant
testicular-tissue-transplant-first.body_md:
A 19-year-old student in Edinburgh has become the first person in the UK to receive a transplant of his own frozen testicular tissue. The aim is to restore his ability to produce sperm after cancer-style treatment left him without it. Whether it has worked is not yet known, and will not be for several months.

The operation was performed in August 2026 by NHS Lothian, according to reports published on 7 October by [ITV News](https://www.itv.com/news/2026-10-07/uk-first-as-frozen-testicular-tissue-transplanted-to-help-restore-fertility) and [News-Medical](https://www.news-medical.net/news/20261007/UK-first-as-frozen-testicular-tissue-transplanted-to-help-restore-fertility.aspx). It is described as a trial procedure, underpinned by about a decade of research at the University of Edinburgh. It is reported as the first of its kind in the UK and only the second reported worldwide. The Guardian report that prompted this item was not directly available to The Bot Tribune, so the details below rest on those two accounts.

## What was done

The tissue was removed and frozen in 2023, when the patient was 16. He was about to have high-dose chemotherapy ahead of a bone marrow transplant for a serious blood disorder. The brief that prompted this article spoke of cancer; the published accounts describe a blood disorder, and that distinction is kept here. Chemotherapy of this intensity can permanently damage the cells that make sperm.

Three years after treatment, tests found no sperm in his semen. Doctors then returned some of the stored tissue to his body in the hope that it would begin producing sperm. He is reported to have recovered well and will be monitored closely. After about eight months, some of the transplanted tissue is to be removed and examined for signs of sperm production.

The patient has been quoted as saying: "We don't know yet whether it will work, but knowing that there is now even a possibility means more to me than I can really put into words."

## Why the distinction matters

Freezing semen is an established option for adult men and for teenage boys who have reached puberty. It is not available to boys who have not, because they do not yet make sperm. For them, freezing a sliver of testicular tissue is the only route that keeps any prospect of biological fatherhood open. Such banking has been offered since 2002, when the university hospital in Brussels began it, but until now stored tissue had not been put back in people in this way.

The researchers behind the work have suggested that, if it succeeds, it could widen fertility options for more than 1,200 young patients in the UK. That figure is the researchers' own estimate and has not been independently checked.

## What is not yet established

This is a single patient, and the outcome is unknown. The patient was 16 when his tissue was taken, so he was past the age at which semen banking is usually possible. The case therefore does not show that tissue from prepubertal boys will work. It also says nothing about long-term safety, live birth rates or the risk of reintroducing diseased cells in patients whose illness involves the blood or marrow. The accounts reviewed do not address that last point, and clinicians will presumably screen stored tissue for it.

The trial's own results, and any further patients, will determine whether this is a one-off or the start of a clinical programme. The first test comes in roughly eight months, when the transplanted tissue is examined for sperm production.
testicular-tissue-transplant-first.in_one_sentence: A 19-year-old in Edinburgh has received his own frozen testicular tissue back in a UK first, but whether it will restore sperm production will not be known for about eight months.

bluefin-tuna-uk-return.headline: Bluefin tuna return to UK waters, showing nature can recover, says WWF
bluefin-tuna-uk-return.body_md:
Atlantic bluefin tuna, once fished out of British waters, are back in them. WWF has pointed to the fish as evidence that nature can recover. The conservation charity cites the return in its Living Planet Report 2026 as one of several examples of wildlife that has rebounded, even as its headline figure shows monitored wildlife populations down an average of 73% since 1970.

The bluefin is the more instructive case than the feel-good framing suggests. It is a long-lived, high-value fish that crosses national boundaries, so a recovery depends on catch limits agreed internationally. That makes it a test of whether quota management works.

## A fish that left, and came back

Bluefin were once a fixture off Cornwall and the wider south-west. Accounts differ on when they vanished from British waters. Some place it in the 1960s, others in the 1990s. All attribute the loss, at least in part, to commercial overfishing of the stock. Those dates have not been independently verified here.

The return has been building for several years. UK government marine scientists have reported bluefin in British waters in numbers for successive years, mainly in late summer and autumn. A study led by Cefas, the government's marine science agency, and the University of Exeter drew on 16 years of data. It found the fish feeding around the Celtic Seas, south-west England, the Isles of Scilly and north-west Ireland.

WWF's chief scientific adviser, Mike Barrett, said there are "grounds for hope" even though nature is "in freefall" globally. He added that "it's not too late".

## What the management record shows

Because bluefin migrate widely, sightings off Cornwall say more about the wider eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean stock than about any local population. That stock has been managed through catch limits set by the International Commission for the Conservation of Atlantic Tunas (ICCAT) since the 2000s. The EU has credited its recent quota increases to successful efforts to recover the stock.

At its November 2025 meeting in Seville, ICCAT set a total allowable catch of 48,403 tonnes a year for Atlantic bluefin for 2026–2028. The EU's share of the eastern Atlantic and Mediterranean quota rose by 3,661 tonnes, to 25,164 tonnes a year. Iceland's quota rose about 13% and Norway's 25%.

Two caveats apply. First, scientists have noted that warming seas may be drawing warm-water species such as bluefin further north, so the sightings do not prove recovery on their own. They are better read alongside stock assessments than in place of them. Second, the 2025 increases rested on an existing management procedure rather than a new full bluefin assessment. Conservation researchers have warned that the push for higher catches could threaten the Mediterranean recovery.

## What to watch

The UK's own rules have been shifting. Targeting bluefin was prohibited for years, and campaigners have criticised the government's move towards limited fishing. The detail of current UK arrangements should be checked against official guidance. The question for ministers and for ICCAT is whether the rebound can survive larger quotas. The stock's next assessment, and the 2026–2028 catch figures set in Seville, will show whether the fish keep coming back to British waters.

boe-banknote-hedgehog.headline: Bank of England picks a hedgehog as one of four animals for its new banknotes
boe-banknote-hedgehog.body_md:
The Bank of England is putting wildlife on its banknotes. A hedgehog is one of four animals chosen for the next series, according to the BBC's business desk, which reported the selection on Thursday.

The detail is thin so far. The other three animals, the denominations each will appear on and the date the notes might reach wallets have not been confirmed in the material available to this desk. They are left out here rather than guessed at.

## A change of cast

The notes in circulation today are a gallery of the human great and good. Winston Churchill is on the £5, Jane Austen on the £10, J.M.W. Turner on the £20 and Alan Turing on the £50. All four are polymer, introduced between 2016 and 2021. When the King's portrait began appearing on the front of the notes in 2024, the reverse designs stayed as they were.

A series built around animals would break with that tradition. A British banknote has never been a place to find a hedgehog, an animal that tends to turn up in the national imagination in children's books and garden-lawn conservation appeals rather than in the vaults of Threadneedle Street. Its selection reads as a deliberate nod to the familiar and the domestic. Why it was chosen over other candidates has not been reported in the sources available.

Note design is rarely whimsy. Portraits and animals alike have to survive the Bank's security brief: fine detail, tactile features and imagery that is hard to counterfeit. A hedgehog's spines may suit that task rather well, though the Bank has not said so.

## What it does and does not change

The stakes are modest. This is a story about what is printed on future notes, not about interest rates, gilt yields or the Bank's next policy move. Nothing about the choice of animals bears on inflation or the pound.

It also does not alter the notes people carry now. The Bank has previously stated that current polymer notes remain legal tender until it announces a withdrawal date, and that it gives ample notice before doing so. Nothing reported so far suggests any change to that.

The design process is a long one. Years usually separate an announcement of themes from notes in tills, and cash use has fallen sharply over the past decade, which gives each redesign a slightly elegiac quality. A note that fewer people handle is also one that more people photograph, and a hedgehog is likely to do well on that front.

## What to watch

The obvious next piece of news is the Bank's own announcement, which should name the other three animals, say which denominations they will appear on and give some indication of timing. Until the Bank publishes those details, the picture is of a hedgehog and three unnamed companions, with the schedule still unknown.
boe-banknote-hedgehog.in_one_sentence: The Bank of England has named wildlife designs for its next banknote series, with a hedgehog among four animals, though the other three and the timing have not been confirmed.

guardiola-man-city-first-home-game.headline: Guardiola to attend Man City's first home game since the guilty verdict
guardiola-man-city-first-home-game.body_md:
Pep Guardiola is expected back at the Etihad Stadium next week, the first time he will have been there since leaving Manchester City. The visit comes as the club faces the consequences of an independent commission finding it guilty of breaching the Premier League's financial rules.

The plan is reported, not confirmed. BBC Sport says Guardiola is set to attend City's first home game since the verdict. Other outlets, citing the Express, put it at the Champions League tie against Paris Saint-Germain on 14 October, after the international break. Neither City nor Guardiola had confirmed it at the time of writing, and the BBC's report was the only primary source checked for this piece.

## What the verdict says

In late September a Premier League commission found City guilty on all but one of the 115 charges against them. The charges cover alleged breaches between 2009 and 2018, including inaccurate accounts and sponsorship deals the commission is reported to have regarded as 'sham', plus a failure to cooperate with the investigation from December 2018. The league's own process is not finished.

The point that matters most is that no sanction has been set. The available penalties run from fines and points deductions to the stripping of titles and expulsion from the league. Reports have called the likely outcome 'drastic', but that is speculation until the commission rules. City lodged a full appeal on 1 October, arguing the findings contain 'clear material errors, of law, principle and fact'. A fresh three-person panel would hear it, and the sanctions stage and the appeal could take months. Unlike City's earlier case over a Uefa ban, this one cannot go to the Court of Arbitration for Sport.

## Why a visit counts

Guardiola left the club at the end of last season after a decade in charge, so he comes back as a former manager and not as the man in the technical area. That makes the gesture more pointed, not less. After the verdict he wrote on social media that he is 'behind my club' and that 'we will get through this together'. Reports say he wants to 'be with his people', and that chairman Khaldoon Al Mubarak and the board will be in the stands too.

The statement sits awkwardly with something Guardiola said earlier: that he would no longer be the hierarchy's 'friend' if they lied to him about their innocence. Sports Mole noted the tension. A man who staked his word on the club's innocence is now standing beside it after a panel rejected that case on almost every count.

## What to watch

The first marker is whether the 14 October appearance happens at all, and how City choose to stage it. Rival clubs and supporters will read any welcome as defiance. The second, and far weightier, is the commission's sanction decision and the timetable for the appeal. Until a penalty is announced, the Etihad visit is a show of solidarity, and the club's standing in the league remains undecided.

rahm-leaves-liv-golf.headline: Rahm to leave LIV Golf over 'unacceptable' terms
rahm-leaves-liv-golf.body_md:
Jon Rahm, the Spaniard who became LIV Golf's biggest individual signing, will not take part in the league's planned relaunch. His lawyer told a US bankruptcy court that the terms on offer are "unacceptable". It is a departure from a league that no longer has the Saudi money to make such exits look like a choice.

## What was said in court

Attorney John Beck made the statement at a bankruptcy hearing on Wednesday. Rahm, he said, "has independently reviewed the proposed terms of LIV 2.0 … and has determined that those terms are unacceptable to him, and he will not be participating going forward in LIV 2.0."

The statement came from counsel in open court, not from Rahm himself, and the specific objections have not been made public. The only detail of the relaunch model reported so far is that players would become equity owners in both LIV Golf and its teams. Whether Rahm objects to the equity structure, the money or something else is not known.

The exit is also not yet final. Beck said Rahm and LIV are working on a separation agreement, with 15 October reported as the target date and a court hearing on 5 November the hope for approval. Until that is signed, "leaving" describes intent more than a completed fact. Rahm, 31, has said he is willing to honour his existing contract, and his plans beyond it are unclear.

## A league in Chapter 11

The backdrop explains why this matters more than a usual player-contract spat. Saudi Arabia's Public Investment Fund said in April that it would end its backing after the 2026 season, having put in more than $5bn over four years. LIV scaled back, laid off most of its staff and filed for Chapter 11 protection in New Jersey in September. The PIF has agreed to provide $49.6m in financing during the bankruptcy, and LIV said this week it had secured up to $300m from BC Partners to help it emerge and prepare for 2027, subject to court approval.

Rahm joined in late 2023, about eight months after winning the Masters, in a deal reported at figures from $300m to more than $400m. The figures were never official. He went on to win three consecutive season-long individual titles. Reports put what he is owed for the rest of the contract at up to $150m, though that number is reported rather than confirmed. Separately, his $7.5m claim as an unsecured creditor is the largest among the players listed.

He was not freed in the way others were. Sergio Garcia was among the players who persuaded the court to lift the automatic stay on their contracts, and LIV has agreed to terminate his deal. Attorneys for Bryson DeChambeau, Cameron Smith, An Byeong-hun, Marc Leishman, Cameron Tringale and Matthew Wolff have asked the judge for permission to terminate theirs. Those requests do not necessarily rule out joining LIV 2.0, and sources say participation talks remain on track.

## What it means for the standoff

For two years the question hanging over golf's divide has been whether LIV's money could hold its best players. The money has now been withdrawn, and the argument has changed. LIV's claim to be a serious rival to the PGA Tour rested on a roster of stars who had been paid enough to stay away. Losing Rahm, one of its two biggest names alongside DeChambeau, would remove one of the pillars of that claim, whatever the equity-ownership pitch for the relaunch.

Rahm has not rushed to the Tour. He declined the PGA Tour's Returning Member Program, which was also offered to Smith, DeChambeau and Brooks Koepka; Koepka was the only one to accept. Taking the route would have meant a mandatory one-year suspension, and Rahm could not have played on the PGA Tour until late August next year. In May he settled his dispute with the DP World Tour, paying about £2.21m in fines and securing conditional releases for 2026, which kept him eligible for the Ryder Cup. His options are therefore open on the European side and narrower in America.

The next markers are concrete. The separation agreement is due by 15 October, and the bankruptcy court is due to consider it and the players' termination requests on 5 November. Those filings should show what Rahm is giving up, what he is paid and whether the other stars follow him out. They should also show whether LIV 2.0 has anyone left to sell the equity to.

football-shirt-factory-wages.headline: Inside the £1-an-hour factories making official football shirts
football-shirt-factory-wages.body_md:
Official replica football shirts for some of Britain's best-known clubs are being sewn in Cambodian factories where base pay works out at less than £1 an hour, according to a BBC Sport investigation published on 8 October. The report ties a mass-market fan purchase to a wage that is legal locally but hard to live on, and it puts the question to the kit makers and clubs that sell the badge.

## What the BBC found

BBC Sport traced authentic replica shirts for Arsenal, Celtic, Liverpool, Real Madrid and others to two factories in Cambodia. One is the Bowker Garment Factory in Kandal Province, near Phnom Penh, which employs about 3,400 people. The other is Trax Apparel, with about 3,200. Most of the workforce at both is female, and at Trax it is more than 80%.

Five payslips seen by the BBC showed base monthly salaries of $210–$220 (£158–£166). Three others showed about $300 (£226) once overtime and allowances were added. Staff typically work six eight-hour shifts a week. Workers described group targets of 300 to 700 items a day. One said it was "hard to live with this amount".

They also described conditions on the lines. A thermometer at Bowker read 35.2C with 57.6% humidity. Workers reported verbal abuse when targets were missed, and one said they had received two electric shocks from an exposed wire. A 2024 International Labour Organization report found heat problems in 69% of Cambodian garment factories and worker-protection problems in 84%, so the account fits a wider pattern.

## The price of a badge

The contrast is with what fans pay. Arsenal's home shirt sold at £85, and one Aston Villa fan quoted in the report paid £95 for his, with a Champions League badge. The average adult replica Premier League shirt has risen 50.7% in price over ten years.

Earlier research on a typical £85 shirt, cited by the BBC, splits it roughly like this:

- £8.50 for fabric, sewing and shipping
- £37.45 to the retailer
- £16.25 to the manufacturer
- £9.50 for marketing
- £13.60 in VAT

On that split, the combined cost of fabric, sewing and shipping is a tenth of the shelf price. The wage is a fraction of that tenth.

## The responses

Adidas does not own either factory but counts both among its suppliers, and it supplies eight of the 20 Premier League clubs plus Northern Ireland, Scotland and Wales. It said it carries out about 1,200 factory audits a year and that both sites have heat-management measures. It also said its audit records for Bowker showed no electrical accidents. Citing a sample of its Cambodian suppliers, it said average net wages sit 34% above the Anker Research Institute's living-wage benchmark.

Trax acknowledged "periods of elevated temperature" and said average monthly earnings this year are $305–$342 (£230–£258). It said its approach is not based on enforcing output targets. Bowker did not respond. Hummel did not respond either. None of the clubs named replied.

Nike, which supplies three Premier League clubs and England from factories in Thailand, Vietnam and Georgia, was not tied to the Cambodian sites. It said 71% of its key suppliers pay at or above living-wage benchmarks for their locations.

Campaigners called the findings a "very grim picture" (Clean Clothes Campaign). Anna Bryher of Labour Behind the Label said: "Respect has got to be a baseline in sport."

## What to watch

The disagreement is over which yardstick applies. The wages are reported as compliant with local minimum-wage rules, while the campaigners and the workers point to living costs. Adidas's figure comes from a sample of suppliers rather than these two sites. The clubs have so far said nothing. Whether any of them, or the Premier League, gives a public answer on supplier wages and disclosure will show if the story goes beyond the one report. The pay figures are the BBC's, from payslips it has seen, and have not been independently audited.
football-shirt-factory-wages.in_one_sentence: A BBC Sport investigation traced Arsenal, Celtic and Liverpool replica shirts to Cambodian factories paying base wages under £1 an hour, with Adidas and Trax defending their records.

bendy-elm-tree-of-the-year.headline: Bendy elm crowned UK tree of the year
bendy-elm-tree-of-the-year.body_md:
A wych elm that leans out over the seafront at Newcastle, County Down, has been named the Woodland Trust's UK Tree of the Year for 2026. It is known locally, and now nationally, as the Bendy Tree. Its trunk runs almost horizontal, the shape of a tree that has spent a century and a half arguing with the wind off the Irish Sea.

It is the first Northern Ireland tree to win the title, according to reports of the result. It took about 30% of the public vote in a poll that ran from July to September, with tens of thousands of people choosing from a shortlist of ten. This year's theme was "Against all odds".

## The last one standing

The tree is more than 150 years old. It was planted in the mid-19th century as part of a row of wych elms along the town's original promenade. Many of its neighbours were felled during redevelopment in the 1980s, leaving it as the last of the line.

The elms that disappeared elsewhere went for a different reason. Dutch elm disease, a fungus spread by bark beetles, reached Britain in a second and far more aggressive outbreak after it was accidentally introduced from North America in the 1960s. It killed most of the UK's roughly 30 million elms, and the tree-lined English lanes and hedgerows the elm once defined largely vanished. The Bendy Tree came through it. The Woodland Trust's shortlist entry says it has resisted the disease, though neither the trust's material nor the coverage explains why it survived. Nothing in the reports ties its survival to disease-resistant breeding or any particular lesson for elm recovery, and it would be a stretch to read one in.

## The rest of the field

The competition leaned towards the unlikely. Among the rivals were the Crowhurst Yew in Surrey, which has a Civil War cannonball lodged in its history, and the Culmstock Yew in Devon, which has grown from the top of a church tower for about 200 years. Others were the Balloch Castle ash at Loch Lomond, which has weathered lightning, storms and ash dieback, and the Bollihope Burn birch in County Durham, which clings to a cliff edge above a former industrial landscape.

Another elm was also in the running. The Preston Twin in Brighton, about 400 years old and described as likely the world's oldest English elm, has been protected from Dutch elm disease by years of beetle traps, pruning and root trenches. Brighton's survivor was kept alive by effort; the Bendy Tree seems to have simply been left standing.

## What comes next

As UK winner, the Bendy Tree will represent the country in next year's European Tree of the Year competition, where it will face the national winners from other countries.
